contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Joan of Arc was a French visionary and military figure whose intervention during the Hundred Years War helped revive the Valois cause at a moment of severe crisis. Claiming guidance from saints, she encouraged the relief of Orleans and supported the coronation of Charles VII at Reims.

Born around 1412 at Domremy, Joan was captured, tried by an English-backed church court, and burned at Rouen in 1431. Her conviction was later overturned, and she became a powerful symbol of faith, resistance, national memory, and the contested politics of sanctity.

Joan's military fame rests on a few decisive months in 1429: she helped lift the Siege of Orléans, which had come to symbolise French collapse in the Hundred Years' War, and days later shared in the crushing victory at the Battle of Patay, before leading Charles VII to his coronation at Reims.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Joan was born around 1412 in Domremy, a village on the frontier of competing loyalties during the later Hundred Years War. Her family were peasants, and her early life was shaped by local warfare, raids, and the political division between Burgundian, English, and Valois forces.

She later testified that she heard voices of saints calling her to aid the French king. Historians can study the trial records, but the inner experience itself remains a matter of belief and interpretation.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Joan of Arc is one of the few medieval figures whose voice survives in something close to her own words, through the transcripts of her trial of condemnation in 1431. Those records, produced by hostile judges trying to destroy her, paradoxically preserve a personality of extraordinary force: defiant, quick-witted, and unshakeably certain of her mission. Her famous answer when asked whether she was in God's grace — a theological trap — has been admired for centuries as a flash of native intelligence under pressure.

The Joan the sources show is devout, disciplined, and physically courageous, insistent on the propriety of her conduct among soldiers, contemptuous of hesitation, and charismatic enough to bend hardened commanders to a peasant girl's conviction. Her certainty about her voices — Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, Saint Margaret — was the core of her, and it never wavered even under the threat of burning.

Her reputation has been pulled in many directions since: heretic, saint, national symbol, and modern icon. But the trial record, read carefully, anchors the personality firmly — a young woman of fierce religious conviction and remarkable presence of mind, whose confidence was inseparable from her belief that she acted on divine command.

contentSections.title: As military figure and visionary
paragraphs: Joan reached the court of Charles VII and was allowed to accompany forces moving to relieve Orleans. Her presence became a rallying symbol, and the lifting of the siege in 1429 helped transform morale.

She then urged the campaign to Reims, where Charles VII was crowned. Although she was not a conventional commander in the modern sense, her authority, symbolism, and persistence had real political and military effects.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Executed by burning at Rouen in 1431 after an ecclesiastical trial shaped by English and Burgundian wartime politics.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Joan of Arc is remembered as a saint, a heroine of France, and one of the most recognizable figures of the Middle Ages. Her image has been used by monarchists, republicans, Catholics, nationalists, feminists, and artists, often for sharply different purposes.
Her history is unusually well documented for a non-elite medieval woman because of trial records, but her reputation has also been heavily romanticized and politicized.

timeline.title: Born
timeline.description: Joan was born at Domremy in a frontier village touched by the violence and loyalties of the Hundred Years’ War.

timeline.title: Reports visionary experiences
timeline.description: Later testimony associates her mission with saints' voices.

timeline.title: Reaches Chinon
timeline.description: Persuades the dauphin's circle to let her join the war effort.

timeline.title: Victory at Patay
timeline.description: Days after the relief of Orléans, the French destroyed the retreating English field army at the Battle of Patay, reversing years of English dominance.

timeline.title: Helps lift the siege of Orleans
timeline.description: Becomes a symbol of French recovery.

timeline.title: Supports coronation at Reims
timeline.description: Charles VII is crowned with Joan present.

timeline.title: Captured at Compiegne
timeline.description: Taken by Burgundian forces and transferred to English custody.
